summary: The northernmost of the three Baltic states; it first became independent in 1918, was annexed by the Soviet Union after World War II, and restored independence in 1991, and is known for e-government and technology startups.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: Estonia is one of the least religious countries in the world. In the 13th century Danish and German crusaders conquered the land by force, and from then on Christianity was linked with the rule of German-descended landlords; the Lutheranism that followed was also led by Baltic German nobles, and Estonian peasants always kept a distance from the church. During the Soviet occupation of 1940–1991, atheism was promoted, church property confiscated and believers suppressed, so the transmission of religion was almost broken, and no return has been seen after independence.

ranking.name: Eastern Orthodoxy
ranking.description: After the Great Northern War in the early 18th century Estonia was incorporated into the Russian Empire, and in the 1840s some Estonian peasants, believing that converting to Orthodoxy would earn them land, converted en masse. During the Soviet period large numbers of Russian-speaking immigrants moved in, which further increased the number of Orthodox believers. Today the believers are mostly Russian-speaking residents of Tallinn and of Ida-Viru County in the northeast, and belong to two churches, the Estonian Apostolic Orthodox Church and the Moscow Patriarchate.

ranking.name: Lutheranism
ranking.description: The Reformation reached Tallinn in the 1520s; after 1561 Sweden ruled northern Estonia, promoting Lutheran education and peasant literacy, and in 1739 the first complete Bible in Estonian was published. Lutheranism was once the main religion of Estonians, but it was severely suppressed in the Soviet period, and the proportion of believers has fallen greatly to the present.

ranking.name: Other Christian
ranking.description: These include Baptists, Pentecostals, Seventh-day Adventists and Catholics, some introduced in the religious revival movements of the late 19th century and driven underground in the Soviet period; today they are not large.

ranking.name: Other religions (including native faiths such as Taara)
ranking.description: In the national movement of the early 20th century “Taaraism” (Taarausk), centered on the ancient Estonian gods, arose and a group was formally founded in 1928; another branch, “Maausk” (Earth Faith), emphasizes the worship of nature and sacred groves. They were banned in the Soviet period and re-registered after independence, and are a symbol of Estonians’ search for a pre-Christian native identity.

religion.background: Estonians originally followed nature worship; in the 13th century the northern crusaders brought Catholicism by conquest, after the Reformation of the 16th century Lutheranism became the mainstream under Swedish rule, and from the 18th century Orthodoxy was introduced with Russian Empire rule. Because the church was long controlled by the foreign ruling class, Christianity has shallow roots among Estonian peasants. Soviet rule from 1940 suppressed religion with atheism, making today’s Estonia one of the most secularized societies in Europe.

ranking.name: Estonian
ranking.description: Estonian belongs to the Finnic branch of the Uralic family, is close to Finnish, and is quite different from the surrounding Indo-European languages. The first book in Estonian (a catechism) was published in 1535 and the complete Bible in 1739; in the national awakening of the 19th century, the epic Kalevipoeg (1857–1861), compiled by Kreutzwald, became a national symbol. After independence in 1918 it became the national language, under the Soviet Union it faced pressure of Russification, and after independence was restored in 1991 it was again established as the sole official language.

ranking.name: Russian
ranking.description: After the Soviet reoccupation in 1944, Moscow moved in large numbers of Russian-speaking workers to develop the oil shale, textile and defense industries of the northeast, and in cities such as Narva and Sillamäe Russian-speakers exceed ninety percent. After independence in 1991 these immigrants and their descendants did not automatically obtain citizenship, and language and citizenship issues have long persisted; from 2024 all schools are gradually switching to instruction in Estonian.

ranking.name: Ukrainian
ranking.description: Some Ukrainian speakers are descendants of workers who moved in during the Soviet period, and others are tens of thousands of refugees who fled to Estonia after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

language.history: The ancestors of the Finnic peoples settled on the eastern shore of the Baltic thousands of years ago. From the 13th century Germans ruled for hundreds of years, Low German became the language of the upper class and brought many loanwords, while Estonian was the spoken language of the peasants. The Reformation and Swedish rule promoted the written use of Estonian, and the national awakening of the 19th century, with newspapers, poetry and song festivals, made it the core of national identity. During Soviet rule from 1940 to 1991 Russian outranked the native language, and after independence was restored Estonian again became the sole official language.

ranking.name: Rye bread (leib)
ranking.description: A dark bread baked from rye flour fermented with sourdough, dense in texture with a slight sourness, sliced thin and eaten with butter, herring or cheese.
ranking.history: Rye adapts to Estonia’s cold, damp climate and for a thousand years has been the peasants’ most important grain, so rye bread is called “the Estonians’ staple.” Traditionally bread was regarded as sacred food, and if it fell on the floor it was picked up and kissed as a sign of respect, and the sourdough starter for baking was passed down through generations. Under German landlords, white bread belonged to the upper classes, while rye bread represented the life and resilience of the peasants, and it is still a must at every meal today.

ranking.name: Verivorst (blood sausage)
ranking.description: A sausage made by stuffing casings with pig’s blood, barley groats, onion and spices such as allspice, heated by roasting and eaten with lingonberry jam, sauerkraut and potatoes.
ranking.history: Traditionally Estonian farm families slaughtered pigs in early winter and made blood and barley into blood sausage to make full use of every part and get through the long winter. Blood sausage is most closely associated with Christmas, and every December supermarkets and households still make large quantities of it, which together with roast pork and sauerkraut makes up the Christmas feast. The lingonberry jam served with it comes from the abundant wild berries of Estonia’s forests.

ranking.name: Kama (roasted grain flour)
ranking.description: A mixed flour ground from roasted barley, rye, oats and peas, stirred into kefir or yogurt, with berries or honey added, for breakfast or dessert.
ranking.history: Kama is a traditional food unique to Estonia, derived from the peasants’ habit of roasting and grinding grain to keep for a long time and carry easily, so that out in the fields they needed only to add sour milk to eat it. In the Soviet period it was made into candies and snacks and is a childhood memory for many. Today it is regarded as one of Estonia’s national foods and is often given as a souvenir representing local cuisine.

ranking.name: Mulgipuder (Mulgi porridge)
ranking.description: Potatoes and barley groats are cooked together until soft and mashed, then topped with fried diced pork belly and onion, creamy, rich and very filling.
ranking.history: The name comes from the Mulgi region of southern Estonia (Mulgimaa, around Viljandi), where in the 19th century farmers grew rich by growing flax and became known for redeeming their land early and valuing education. After potatoes arrived in the 18th century they were combined with the traditional barley into this farm dish, which is both cheap and filling. It is regarded as representative of the local culture of southern Estonia, and in recent years has also become a signature dish of restaurants promoting local food.

ranking.name: Kohuke (sweet curd snack)
ranking.description: Sweetened curd (quark cheese) is pressed into small bars and coated with a layer of chocolate, sold chilled, with a cold, creamy texture and a moderate sweet-and-sour taste.
ranking.history: Sweet curd bars began to be industrially produced across the Baltics and Eastern Europe in the Soviet period, and with Estonia’s well-developed dairy industry, curd desserts quickly became a popular snack. Cheap and available in many flavors, they are often bought as a snack by everyone from students to office workers. Today brands offer dozens of flavors, and they are among the most representative products in the chilled cabinets of Estonian supermarkets.
